## Summary

A plain comment on a GitHub issue now answers the factory's question. One recognition rule, `github_factory.admit_answer_notice`, serves both the signed webhook and the poll pass, then hands the comment to the answer core (`factory_questions.admit_answer`). A comment on an issue whose question round is `outstanding` or `answered` is an answer first, with or without a mention, and never also a mention revision. It must come from a `User` acting directly or through another GitHub App (not the factory's own App), whose effective permission is write, maintain or admin, on an issue a fresh App read shows open and still carrying the WorkItem's trigger label. The comment's author, App provenance, issue and creation time come from the factory's own authenticated read (the poll listing, or a comment read for a webhook). Refusals are logged by reason code and identifiers only (`answer_from_bot`, `answer_not_authorized`, `ticket_closed`, `trigger_label_absent`, and the core's outcomes). A comment that is not an answer is refused exactly as before (`ordinary_comment`, `app_authored`, `sender_mismatch`), and edits stay `unsupported_action`. The GitHub issue read now keeps the newest 1,000 comments of a longer thread.

Decisions taken where the contract left room:

1. Posting-state recovery. An answer seen while the round still reads `posting` (its question comment is on the ticket but not yet recorded `outstanding`) used to get a permanent `not_outstanding` receipt from the answer core. `_decide` now refuses it with `question_posting` before writing anything, under the WorkItem lock, so it also covers a round that moved from `answered` to a new round's `posting` after the intake looked. The intake turns that into a retry: the webhook answers 503 and the delivery audit stays `retryable`, so a redelivery of the same delivery admits it; the poll pass keeps an `answer-retry:<comment id>` cursor key and decides the comment on a later pass. The answer core's own test for the `posting` case now asserts the raise and no receipt.
2. Webhook mode has no poll pass and GitHub never redelivers a 503 by itself, so a deferred webhook answer also records an `answer-retry:<comment id>` key in the scope's poll cursor, added atomically. The poll pass drains those keys in poll mode. In webhook mode a new work item reconciler step, `drain_answer_retries`, drains them on every tick, independent of the label sweep's interval, and costs one query when no key is held. The poll pass never writes or drops these keys when it saves its own cursor, so a key a webhook adds during a poll pass survives it. The step is declared in the telemetry step domain.
3. A Slack kickoff WorkItem has no trigger label and no label removal cancels it (#5380), so only the open check applies to answers on it; refusing them would strand a kickoff run's questions, whose comment tells the reporter to answer plainly. A closed issue still refuses. A reviewer read decision 3 as requiring a label here; this is left for the maintainer.
4. As for a mention, an answer is refused `binding_missing` when the WorkItem's agent no longer has a GitHub surface on the repository and `installation_mismatch` when it arrives from another installation. A comment that already has an answer receipt replays before any other check and any GitHub read, so a mention that answered is never admitted again as a mention after its round clears, and a poll pass interrupted by its deadline re-reads admitted answers cheaply. On an issue with an open round, the poll pass skips any comment it lists with an `updated_at` later than its `created_at`, or created before its listing threshold, so an edit never becomes an answer, even one made before the pass first saw the comment (a facts request edited into plain text), matching the webhook's `unsupported_action`. A body the facts exchange accepts on the authenticated read is never an answer. A comment edited within the cursor's own second is skipped too, while a new reply created in that second is still read. In personal mode an answer on a WorkItem the owner did not start is refused before any GitHub read, as a mention would be.
6. Rolling upgrade. While an older API replica still serves, a plain answer that reaches it is refused there as an ordinary comment, as today, and is not read again; the person answers again or mentions the App. The answer core's guard (`test_factory_question_mixed_version.py`) now lists the intake as a reader of the round state, and a new case proves that an answer reaching a new replica after an older replica settled the asker is the round's one continuation. Recovering answers an older replica dropped would need a backfill read of the issue after the roll; not built, recorded here for the maintainer.
5. Issue read order. Decision 9 says "the 10 pages ending at the last page", which for a thread whose last page is partial returns fewer than 1,000 comments; acceptance criterion 8 requires the newest 1,000. The read follows the criterion: it reads one earlier page when the last page is partial and keeps the newest 1,000 (at most 12 comment page requests, counting page 1). A `rel="next"` without a `rel="last"` is followed forward as before within ten pages and refused as unavailable beyond them. `IssueContent.comments_truncated` is renamed `earlier_comments_omitted`; its one reader writes `_Earlier comments were not read._` after the description, and `_Later comments were not read._` is no longer written.

5. The immediate and late cases run on both paths with real numeric comment ids: a reply in the question comment's own second with the next id admits one request; an older comment delivered after the question admits none.

Each test drives the production caller: signed `POST /github/webhook` deliveries or a real poll pass, with the question posted through the questions route by the real GitHub tracker into the GitHub fake. The GitHub fields relied on (`issue_comment` action, `performed_via_github_app`, `user.type`, issue `state`, the comments listing `Link` header) are cited to GitHub's REST and webhook documentation in the tests.

## Summary

Adds the scripted `one-ticket` scenario to the scripted kind command. After the publication scenario passes, one human label goes on one fresh GitHub issue in the stub and the flow is observed from outside: the factory says it is investigating, session 1 asks two numbered questions on the ticket with `ask_questions`, a read-permission comment and a bot comment start nothing, the labeller's plain answer starts a second request that says `Answer received.`, session 2 opens exactly one pull request that closes the issue, the factory creates no issue of its own, and a second plain comment posted with the answer starts nothing more. Only the model and GitHub boundaries are scripted; the assertions read the stub and read-only SQL (WorkItems, requests, question rounds and answer receipts). The verdict lands under `one_ticket` in the scripted evidence file and decides the command's exit code.

Supporting changes: a new scripted transcript and fixture issue, stub helpers to append never-edited comments (one transaction, one instant) and to add a user with a permission, a stub history of every body a comment held so status lines are placed in time by the comment that carried them, and a lane router that can serve one agent's lanes without per-agent markers.

Discovery waiver: #5808

Findings recorded for the reviewer:

1. After a question round the worker sends one continuation prompt to an implementation turn that ended without publishing (`_continue_unpublished`), so the scripted session 1 ends twice, on its questions and on that continuation. This is the existing behavior, not changed here.
2. The two human comments are posted together and intake commits each answer separately. If the dispatch of the second request began between those two commits, the follow-up would queue a third request instead of coalescing and the scenario would fail loudly with the receipt outcome named. The window is a few milliseconds against a dispatch that takes seconds, and closing it needs a product hook that holds the request waiting, so it is left open rather than added.

## Summary

<!-- One paragraph: what changed, and why. Skip the play by play. -->

The default factory bundle now investigates before it pins criteria and asks questions on the ticket instead of ending with a prose list. A new `investigate` phase sits directly after `read_issue` in the skill and in `phases.json`, with its own `Investigating the ticket` stage. A missing decision is asked with `mcp__curie__ask_questions` after at least one shell probe, and the ticket thread, including the factory's earlier question comments, is the specification on the next attempt. The triage reproduction gate moves into the bundle with `git mv` and is retargeted to enforce three rules without blocking the build: ask only after a recorded probe, never publish after a recorded ask, and cite answers read from the ticket in the Decisions section. Its registration is appended after the review gate entries, which are untouched. The moved evals now judge `ask` or `build` outcomes, the triage bundle loses its hooks and evals, the embedding list and render modes follow, and the bundle text names GitHub, GitLab and Jira Cloud instead of a GitHub issue.

Decisions made while building, each recorded for review:

1. `investigate` is the second phase, directly after `read_issue` (decision 1). `pin_criteria` joined the `plan` stage in `phases.json` because stages must cover every phase in order.
2. The review gate refuses a Decisions line that is not a numbered entry, so the citation is written as an unnumbered line `Answered on the ticket by <author>: <the decision>`, one per answer relied on. `decisions_section.py` accepts those lines outside the seven-entry cap, so no run can drop a citation.
3. The hook lists its state directory in the repository `info/exclude`, so the state never joins the published candidate, and it resolves the checkout root once per event so a shell `cd` cannot split its state.
4. A missing service, credential or tool is a run reason (`Could not complete:`), not a question, so the `capability-unavailable` eval case was removed.
5. A `get_issue` result larger than the hook's input limit, or replaced by Claude Code with an overflow notice, is recorded as carrying the question heading, so publication still needs the citation lines. Citation state survives checkout cleanup. The input limit itself is unchanged.
6. The `question-format.md` grader file still lists a `working_database` need value that no case uses. Removing it changes the prompt of every recorded response, so it is left for a follow-up.
7. Recorded evals were re-recorded where the skill edits changed their prompt hash, each from a fresh Claude child context on the rendered prompt.

## Summary

Part 1 of 2 of #5808 (the live GitHub chain proof). Adds the pure judge for every beat and bound of decision 7, the spend, attempt and teardown verdicts of decisions 8 and 10, the evidence sanitizer of decision 9, the fixture texts of decision 3 and a fully passing record set. `judge_chain` takes already fetched records as plain data (GitHub API JSON, CLI JSON, install records, timings) and returns one verdict per beat with reasons; it does no network, subprocess, cluster or file access. The driver, the scenario registration, the seed issue change, the docs paragraph and the live run are part 2 and are not in this change.

Record shapes of features that are not merged yet are each isolated in one small named constant or parser marked `ASSUMED` in `tools/factory-e2e/live_github_chain_judge.py`, so part 2 adjusts them in one place:

1. `TOOL_NOTES_KEY`, `PROPOSE_RULE_TOOL` and `revision_request_id` (#5794 decision 2.2, #5796 decisions 5 and 11): the request's tool trajectory is a `tool_notes` list of names or `{tool|name}` mappings; the revision request id is `uuid5(NAMESPACE_URL, "curie-review:<repository id>:<pr>:<review id>")`.
2. `review_url` (#5794 decision 2.5): the rule's `source_url` is `<repository URL>/pull/<n>#pullrequestreview-<review id>`.
3. `RULES_KEY` and the rule states (#5797 decision 1): the `curie cluster memory --rules --json` output holds its rules under `rules`. #5797 does not name the top-level key; this is a guess to confirm when it lands.
4. `refusal_code` and `READER_REFUSAL_CODES` (#5797 decisions 3 and 7): a refusal prints `{"error","fix"}` with the `memory_rules.*` code inside `error`.
5. `accepted_rule_of` and `principal_of` (#5797 decisions 1 and 2): the accept and remove output is the changed rule item, with `accepted_by` as `{principal_id, display_name}`.
6. `work_item_rules_of` and `LEARNED_RULES_LINE` (#5798 decisions 2 and 9): the work item read carries `memory_rules: {state, count, rule_numbers, sha256, format_version}`, and the pull request line is `Learned rules: in force; rules:R1; sha256:<digest>` directly before the `Requester preferences:` line.
7. `deploy_refusal_codes` and `BUNDLE_RETIRED_CODE` (#5804 decision 3): a refused deploy reports `bundle.result_declaration_retired` as a `code` field at any depth.
8. `ACTIVE_REQUEST_STATES` (#5803, #5790): the request states meaning queued or in progress are `queued` and `running`, as decision 7 states them.
9. `ANSWERED_PREFIX` (#5790 decision 4) and the `Closes #<n>` rule: the `Answered on the ticket by ` line must sit under a markdown heading named Decisions, matched with an optional list marker.
10. Request records carry `work_item_id` and `finished_at` (null while active); the judge uses them to tie evidence to ticket A's work item and to find the requests active 60 seconds after the questions. Not named by an issue; the install's request read must supply them.
11. Usage is sampled under the labels `before_a` and `after_a` to `after_h`; the 50 USD cap applies to every sample. Label events use GitHub's timeline shape (`event`, `label.name`, `actor`, `created_at`), and review reads carry `pull_request_url` and comments `pull_request_review_id`.

No two issues contradicted each other on a shape the judge needs. Also assumed, from decision 7: the reader permission refusal set is `write` and `admin` as the ticket words it (a `maintain` permission is not refused). The sanitizer matches identifiers literally and percent-encoded once (`%2d`, `%39`); double encoding is not covered.

## Summary

A proposed learned rule can now be accepted, rejected or removed by a person who can merge in its repository, through the memory API and `curie cluster memory`. `GET /agents/{agent_id}/memory/rules` lists proposed, accepted, rejected and removed rules (never candidate, superseded or discarded) for the platform key or a console session. `POST /agents/{agent_id}/memory/rules/{rule_id}/accept`, `/reject` and `/remove` take a console session only, with the same origin check and no platform key. A repository rule is decided only when the principal's one active GitHub identity link on the scope's host can write to the repository, read from the code host at the time of the action: the repository is resolved by the immutable id in its scope key, its kind, host and id must match the scope, and only then is the permission read on the path the resolution returned, never on the stored label. Accept is capped at 16 accepted rules per scope and at the 4096 byte snapshot bound the apply step enforces, counted under a lock on the agent row. Each decision is a compare and set on the rule version, stamps the person and the database clock, and writes one `memory_rule_events` row in the same transaction. The response carries `applies_from: "next_ticket"`.

Output shapes. `GET /agents/{agent_id}/memory/rules` and `curie cluster memory <agent> --rules --json` return one object: `rules` (the list, each item with `id`, `number`, `label`, `scope_kind`, `scope_key`, `scope_label`, `state`, `text`, `reason`, `source_url`, `proposed_by`, `proposed_at`, `accepted_by`, `rejected_by` and `removed_by` as `{principal_id, display_name}` or null, `accepted_at`, `rejected_at`, `removed_at`, `version`), `scopes` (one entry per returned scope with `in_force_count`, the accepted count regardless of the state filter) and `in_force_limit: 16`. An action returns `{"rule": <item>, "applies_from": "next_ticket"}`. The CLI validates both responses against these shapes and prints them; a response in another shape exits 1 naming the field path that differs. A field the API always sends, even as null, must be present: a missing `accepted_by` is refused by name, an explicit null is accepted. A refusal body is `detail: {code, message, fix}` (plus `current_version`, `limit` or `limit_bytes` where they apply); the CLI prints it as `{"error": "<code>: <message>", "fix": "<fix>"}` and exits 1.

Refusal codes: 401 for the platform key, an `Authorization` header or any other credential header on an action; 403 from the console origin check; 404 `memory_rules.not_found` (other tenant, unknown agent or rule); 403 `memory_rules.scope_not_supported` (agent and binding scope); 403 `memory_rules.write_access_required` (no link, an account without write, an unknown account id, a permission payload for another id); 403 `memory_rules.write_access_unverifiable` (a `path:` or non numeric project id, a kind with no identity namespace, no configured code host for the host, two links on one host, an id that no longer resolves or resolves to another repository); 503 `memory_rules.code_host_unavailable`; 409 `memory_rules.stale_version` with `current_version`, `memory_rules.invalid_transition`, `memory_rules.scope_full` with `limit: 16`, `memory_rules.snapshot_full` with `limit_bytes: 4096`; 422 `memory_rules.invalid_request`.

2. The GitHub adapter needs a path to mint the credential for an id read, so the stored label is passed only as that hint. Identity comes from `GET /repositories/{id}`, and the permission read uses the path that call returned.

5. The learned rule verbs have their own CLI output type and schema, `cli/schema/memory-rules.schema.json` v1.0, so `memory.schema.json` v2.2 is unchanged.
6. An action re-reads, under the identity reader fence and in the decision's own transaction, the exact identity link the code host check used. A link revoked or changed while the code host was being read refuses with `memory_rules.write_access_required` and changes nothing.

## Summary

A factory revision run admitted from reviewer feedback can now propose one learned rule for its repository, and the rule stays hidden until the pull request settles (ADR 0287). The runner mounts a `propose_rule` tool only when the completion contract offers it (`rule_proposal: true`) and the model is real; the tool posts only `rule` and `reason` to the new `POST /work-items/rule-proposal`, a sibling of the issue read authorized by the same execution scoped `wir` capability. The API stores one hidden `candidate` per execution request, taking the agent, repository scope key, scope label, source request, source lineage, source URL and proposer from the verified capability and the stored request, never from the body. Every terminal write of a pull request lineage settles its candidates in the same transaction through one shared function: a merge promotes the newest to `proposed` with the next number in its scope and supersedes the rest, a close discards them. Operators turn it on with `curie cluster overrides <agent> --memory-rule-proposals on` (`PATCH /agents/{id}` `memory_rule_proposals`), and the implement-issue skill tells a revision run when to call the tool.

Decisions beyond the issue text, each recorded here:

1. Decision 8 named two terminal lineage writers; there are four on this base. Settlement runs in all of them: the two in `crud/lineages.py`, the never-pushed lineage retirement close in the same file, and the worker's `PostgresPublicationStore.mark_lineage_terminal`, which writes merged or closed by raw SQL. The settlement SQL therefore lives once in `curie_internal.memory_rules.settle_lineage_candidates`, and `memory_rule_lifecycle.settle_lineage_rule_candidates` (the name the issue gives) delegates to it.
2. Rolling upgrade: a replica built before this change records a merge or close without settling. The lineage reconciler pass now also settles up to 50 merged or closed lineages that still hold candidates, each in its own transaction. Every API process also runs that sweep as its own task (`start_rule_settlement`), every `memory_rule_settlement_interval_s` (default 60, no off value), whatever `CURIE_WORK_ITEM_RECONCILER_ENABLED`, the factory switch or the forge pass interval say: those switches still gate only the forge pass, never settlement, since an older replica's publication advance can record a merge or close with no forge pass at all. Candidate rows are locked `FOR UPDATE` and updated only while still `candidate`, so two replicas settle a lineage once.
3. Locking: number allocation takes a transaction advisory lock keyed on the agent and scope, not a row lock on the agent as decision 8 says, because a settlement holding the lineage row and then waiting on the agent row deadlocks with agent deletion (which holds the agent row and then cascades to the lineage). The proposal and every terminal writer take the agent row `FOR KEY SHARE` first, matching deletion's order.
4. Acceptance criterion 1, cancelled work item: a work item already cancelled when the runner asks keeps the existing 409 `invalid_context` from the completion contract, because answering 200 would weaken the fence that keeps a cancelled run's model from starting; every refusal body of that route now also carries `rule_proposal: false`, and the runner still refuses to start on it. A cancellation that lands after that fence and before the eligibility read is answered 200 with `rule_proposal: false`. Both are tested through the real route.
5. A request with no stored `requester` is ineligible (the proposer column is NOT NULL). Beyond decision 2, the proposal itself passes the issue read route's running fence (`read_issue_authority(..., running=True)`: running, runtime owner, unexpired heartbeat lease and deadline), because a finished revision's capability still verifies and a late call could otherwise store a candidate that supersedes the live revision's on merge. The completion contract's offer does not demand a running execution, since the runner reads it at boot before the start. A database failure while storing answers 503 `rule_proposal_unavailable` and drops the database error, whose message displays the bound rule and reason.
6. A `retired_contract` contract may also mount the tool when the API offers it.
7. `propose_rule` is side effecting and its arguments are withheld from the action frame and the transcript record, as `ask_questions` is, so neither a candidate nor text the API refused is readable through the action ledger.
8. `curie local overrides` did not get the flag; decision 9 names only the cluster command.
9. The overrides CLI schema moves to v4 (a new required field), with its baseline and index refreshed.
10. Not done: an index on candidate rows by source lineage (a review advisory for the sweep's lookup) needs a migration, which this ticket does not add. The new route path joins the telemetry route domain. The implement-issue skill sentence changes the prompt hashes of three recorded plan-policy eval replies; they were re-recorded through that eval's own render and record commands, one fresh child context each.

Optional review note not taken: the runner-to-API handoff test rebuilds the capability header and route rather than forwarding the runner's own. Rebased onto `next` before the final push.

Shared files with #5797 (accept, reject and remove routes, building in parallel): this PR does not touch `routers/memory_rules.py` or the `--rules` CLI surface. Both regenerate `apps/api/openapi.json`, the UI API types and the command manifests, so whichever merges second regenerates once after rebasing.

## Summary

<!-- One paragraph: what changed, and why. Skip the play by play. -->

A ticket's accepted learned rules now apply to the next factory ticket for that repository. Admission pins the accepted rules (numbers, canonical text, digest) at the first admission of a work item, in the same transaction as the requester selection, and every request of that work item copies a pending evidence marker. A rule accepted or removed afterwards changes only the next work item. The worker delivers the pinned rules to the implementer's runner in a version 1 envelope beside the requester envelope (ADR 0278 stays untouched), the runner verifies it against the bound execution and the digest, acknowledges, and renders the rules between the bundle prompt and the requester preferences. The pull request carries a platform written line naming rule numbers and the digest. Decisions taken in this run:

1. A repository scope that would not fit its bounds (over 16 accepted rules or over 4096 canonical bytes) refuses admission with 409 memory_rules_unavailable and writes nothing. The accept route keeps a scope inside both bounds, so this is a backstop; both edges have boundary tests.
2. Only an implementation request is served the rules. A request under another completion contract (the separate triage path, which ADR 0286 leaves unextended) carries evidence none and is served an absent envelope.
3. The requester framing gains the learned rules entry only when a learned rules section is in the prompt, so with no rules the whole prompt is byte identical to before.
4. The rule text rides the implementer's system prompt, so the transcript checkpoint can retain it, exactly as requester preferences already do under ADR 0278. A reviewer objected; it is documented in docs/operations.md and not changed here.
5. An older worker that never delivers the envelope blocks the start offline, and the explanation names missing_envelope.
